p1.title: Passage 1
paras: The traveller of earlier centuries set out with little more than a letter of introduction and a vague idea of the road. Delays were expected, routes changed with the weather, and much of what was seen had not been seen before by anyone the traveller knew. Today a journey can be planned to the hour. Reviews tell us where to eat, photographs show us in advance what each monument will look like, and a phone in the pocket ensures that we need never be lost. Few would wish to give up these conveniences, which have made travel safer and open to far more people than ever before.

Yet a journey fully known in advance risks becoming a kind of verification: we go to confirm that the place matches its picture. The encounters that travellers most often remember, by contrast, are the unplanned ones, such as the conversation with a stranger on a delayed train, the festival stumbled upon in a small town, or the meal in a house where no menu existed. These cannot be booked, only allowed for. The thoughtful traveller therefore leaves some of the day unscheduled and some of the map blank, not out of carelessness but as a deliberate act of openness. To travel well is not merely to arrive where one intended, but to be willing, now and then, to arrive somewhere one did not.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: Elections are the most visible moment of a democracy, and the long queues outside polling booths are rightly celebrated. But a citizen who votes once in five years and attends to public affairs at no other time has exercised only a small part of the role. Between elections, the decisions that most affect daily life are taken in municipal councils, village assemblies, school committees and government offices, often in meetings that few citizens attend and through documents that few read. Where the public is absent, those with organised interests, whether contractors, landlords or particular lobbies, are not.

Active citizenship asks more. It includes knowing who one's representatives are and what they have done, attending a ward or gram sabha meeting, using the right to information, and joining with neighbours to raise a common grievance. None of this requires exceptional virtue, but it does require time and a degree of confidence that many people, burdened by work and wary of officialdom, lack. A healthy democracy therefore depends not only on the conscientiousness of individuals but on institutions that make participation practical: meetings held at convenient hours, notices in plain language, and officials who treat questions as a right rather than an annoyance. Democracy, in this sense, is less an event than a habit, and habits must be cultivated.

questions.q: The main idea of the passage is that:
opts: Earlier travellers were careless and ill-prepared.
Travel is safer today than ever before.
Modern planning has real value, but leaving room for the unplanned enriches travel.
Modern travel conveniences should be abandoned.
questions.why: Main idea: few would give up conveniences, yet 'the thoughtful traveller... leaves some of the day unscheduled'.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as an example of a memorable unplanned encounter?
opts: A guided tour of a famous monument.
A festival stumbled upon in a small town.
A hotel room booked months ahead.
A photograph taken at a famous viewpoint.
questions.why: Detail: 'the festival stumbled upon in a small town'.

questions.q: By calling a fully planned journey "a kind of verification", the author implies that such travellers:
opts: Write reviews for other travellers.
Go mainly to confirm what they already expect to see.
Prove that earlier travellers were wrong.
Check the accuracy of their travel documents.
questions.why: Inference: 'we go to confirm that the place matches its picture'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards modern travel conveniences is:
opts: Appreciative, but cautious about relying on them entirely.
Wholly hostile.
Entirely uncritical.
Indifferent.
questions.why: Tone: they 'made travel safer and open to far more people', yet a fully known journey 'risks becoming a kind of verification'.

questions.q: The word "deliberate" in "a deliberate act of openness" most nearly means:
opts: Careless
Slow
Accidental
Intentional
questions.why: Vocabulary: contrasted with 'not out of carelessness'; the blank map is chosen on purpose.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: Why Officials Dislike Questions
A History of the Gram Sabha
The Mechanics of the Polling Booth
Democracy Between Elections
questions.why: Main idea: citizenship must continue between elections, where most decisions are taken.

questions.q: According to the passage, when the public is absent from local decision-making:
opts: Officials take no decisions at all.
Elections are held earlier than planned.
Those with organised interests, such as contractors and landlords, are still present.
Meetings are cancelled for lack of attendance.
questions.why: Detail: 'Where the public is absent, those with organised interests... are not'.

questions.q: The passage suggests that many people do not participate actively mainly because they:
opts: Are forbidden from attending meetings.
Are uninterested in public affairs.
Believe voting is unimportant.
Lack time and confidence, not because they lack virtue.
questions.why: Inference: participation 'does not require exceptional virtue, but it does require time and a degree of confidence that many people... lack'.

questions.q: The author mentions "meetings held at convenient hours" and "notices in plain language" in order to show that:
opts: Citizens should write the notices themselves.
Officials are mainly to blame for every problem.
Institutions can make participation practical for ordinary people.
Meetings should be held only at night.
questions.why: Purpose: they illustrate 'institutions that make participation practical'.

questions.q: The statement "Democracy... is less an event than a habit" means that democracy:
opts: Happens automatically once a constitution exists.
Depends on continuing participation, not only on periodic voting.
Consists chiefly of election day celebrations.
Is a tradition that cannot be changed.
questions.why: Inference: contrasts the 'event' of elections with ongoing civic practice that 'must be cultivated'.
